the guru, his face joyful, endowed with every auspicious thing and having performed his daily rites, should enter the house of worship.
Having performed the great worship of Mahesha in the middle of the mandala, he should again invoke Shiva in the Shiva pot and worship him.
Having examined the ground according to rule by smell, colour, taste and the like, he should construct a pavilion there by the path described in the shastra of craftsmen.
Meditating on the Lord, protector of the sacrifice, as facing west, he should worship the weapon of the Lord in the weapon vessel to the south of the Lord.
Placing the mantra in the mantra pot, the one skilled in mantras, having made the gestures and the rest, should perform the mantra sacrifice.
Then the excellent teacher should make the fire offering in the Shiva fire; other brahmins should make offerings around the principal fire-pit.
Their offering is prescribed as a quarter or half of the teacher's; then the excellent teacher should make offerings in the principal fire-pit itself.
Others should do Vedic recitation, hymns and auspicious recitation, and others devoted to Shiva should do japa according to rule.
Having had dance, song, music and other auspicious things performed, and the members of the assembly properly honoured according to rule,
and having the auspicious day proclaimed and again worshipped Shankara, the teacher should entreat the god, wishing grace for the disciple:
Be gracious, lord of the god of gods; entering my body, release this one, lord of the universe, in your mercy, O treasury of mercy.
Then, saying "I shall do so," and having received permission, the teacher should bring the disciple, who has fasted, or eaten only sacrificial food,
or taken a single meal, abstinent, bathed, having performed the morning rites, reciting the pranava, meditating on the god, having done auspicious things.
Having made an altar, he should arrange fire-pits in its middle, in the eight directions or in the four, and again in the north-east in order.
At the front of the western door of the mandala, or of the southern, having seated the novice on a darbha seat facing north,
himself standing facing east, with the disciple's body erect and hands folded, sprinkling him on the head with the sprinkling water with the weapon gesture,
striking him with a toss of flowers, the guru should bind his eyes with half a fine cloth, new and consecrated with mantras.
Then the guru should lead the disciple into the mandala through the door, and he, directed by him, should circumambulate Shambhu three times.
Then, offering the lord a handful of flowers mixed with gold, facing east or north he should prostrate on the ground like a staff.
Then, sprinkling him on the head with the root mantra and striking him with the weapon mantra as before, the teacher should release his blindfold.
Seeing the mandala, he should again bow to the lord with folded hands. Then the Shaiva teacher, seated to the south of the mandala,
having seated the disciple on his left on a darbha seat and worshipped Mahadeva, should place upon him the hand of Shiva.
Regarding his hand as made of Shiva's radiance, he should utter the Shiva mantra, and, filled with the conviction that he is Shiva, place it on the disciple's head.
With that same hand the teacher should touch all his limbs; and the disciple should bow on the ground to the Lord in the form of the teacher.
He should make the principal fire-pit, or else on the western side; or, making only the principal one, he should arrange the decoration.
Then, having worshipped the god in the Shiva fire according to rule and offered three oblations, seating the disciple as before,
touching him with the tips of darbha grass, he should enter him through knowledge; bowing to Mahadeva, he should perform the joining of the channels.
Having made the breath go out by the path described in the Shiva shastras, and remembering its entry into the disciple's body, he should satisfy the mantras.
For the satisfying of the root mantra, ten oblations should be given with it, and three each for the limbs with the limb mantras in order.
Then, having given the full oblation, the teacher who knows the mantras should for atonement make ten more oblations with the root mantra.
Having again worshipped the lord of gods and sipped water properly, and having made offerings as is right, the teacher should raise a vaishya from his own caste;
in the same way he should produce his kshatriya status and raise him again; and in the same way the teacher should produce his brahmin status.
Having thus raised a kshatriya and made him a brahmin, he should produce Rudra-hood in the brahmin and establish him with Rudra's name.
Having sprinkled and struck the novice, remembering his own self in himself as of the nature of Shiva, flashing like a spark,
the guru should expel the breath with mantra through the channel described; going out, he should enter the disciple's channel and then his heart.
With canopies, banners and garlands of many kinds in abundance; then in the middle of the altar he should make a mandala with auspicious marks,
Entering, remembering his consciousness as like a blue dot, he should contemplate it as blazing, its impurity dispelled by his own radiance.
Taking it by that channel with the gesture of withdrawal, the mantra-knower should, with inhalation, place it in himself for the sake of oneness.
With retention, and with exhalation through the channel as before, taking it from there, he should place it in the disciple's heart.
Touching him and giving him the sacred thread obtained from Shiva, having offered three oblations, he should then give the full oblation.
Seating the disciple on an excellent seat to the right of the god, spread with kusha and flowers, facing north with folded hands,
in the svastika posture, himself facing east, seated on an excellent seat, with mantras and the sounds of great auspiciousness,
taking up the full pot, fully prepared, meditating on Shiva, the teacher should sprinkle the disciple.
Then, wiping off the bath water and putting on a white garment, having sipped water and been adorned, the disciple should go to the pavilion with folded hands.
Seating him as before on a darbha seat, the guru should worship the god in the mandala and perform the placing on the hands.
Then the teacher, meditating on the god in his mind, should touch the novice with both hands with ash and utter "Shiva."
with powders of red, gold and other colours fit for invoking the Lord; or, if poor, with powders of vermilion, rice and wild rice.
Then the Shaiva teacher, having performed for him the burning, flooding and the rest, and the making whole by the path of placing the letters,
then contemplating Shiva's seat on the disciple's head, the teacher should invoke Shiva there as is right and worship him mentally.
With folded hands he should entreat the god, "Abide here always"; having made this request, he should remember him shining with Shambhu's radiance.
Then, having worshipped Shiva and received Shiva's command, which is of Shiva's nature, he should softly utter the Shiva mantra into the disciple's ear.
The disciple, with folded hands, hearing the mantra with his mind absorbed in it, should softly repeat it at the command of the Shaiva teacher.
Then, the one skilled in mantras, having taught the Shakti mantra too and had him utter it easily, should bless him with auspiciousness.
Then, having taught briefly the meaning of the mantra through the relation of denoted and denoting, and the form of the Lord, he should teach yoga and posture.
Then, by the guru's command, in the presence of Shiva, the fire and the guru, the disciple, resolving thus with devotion, should utter the words of initiation:
Better that I give up my life, or even that my head be cut off, than that I should eat without worshipping the blessed three-eyed one.
He should keep this vow until the reversal of delusion; until then he should worship the god, established in him and devoted to him.

Then he will be called a samayin in Shiva's order; having gained eligibility, he should keep the guru's command and be subject to him.
After this, placing his hand on him and taking ash in his own hand, he should give it to the disciple with the root mantra, and a consecrated rudraksha,
an image of the god or a hidden emblem, and, if possible, the means of worship, fire offering, japa and meditation.
That disciple too should accept with great honour what he receives from the Shaiva teacher, by the teacher's command and not otherwise.
Placing all that he has received from the teacher on his head with devotion, he should keep it and worship Shambhu in a monastery or at home.
After this the teacher should teach him Shiva's conduct according to his devotion, faith and understanding.
Whatever was said, whatever was enjoined and whatever else was proclaimed by the Shaiva teacher at the samaya rite, he should bear on his head.
The taking up, reading and hearing of Shiva's Agama he should do at the teacher's direction, not of his own will nor from another.
Thus in brief has been told the sacrament called samaya, the supreme means for men to reach Shiva's city directly.

Having made it rich in decoration and ornament, he should arrange to its north-east another mandala of one cubit or half that on the altar.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 17: the description of the rite of Shiva initiation. Upamanyu said: After this, having examined the disciple's fitness, the guru should perform the purification of the six paths for release from all bonds.
cannot even know their pervading and pervaded relation. Therefore, having properly understood the nature of the paths and their pervading and pervaded relation,
he should perform the purification of the paths. Having made everything up to the fire-pit and mandala as before,
he should make a pot-mandala two cubits in size in the east. Then the Shaiva teacher, bathed, with the disciple, having performed the daily rites,
should enter the mandala and worship Shambhu as before. There, sweet rice cooked with no less than an adhaka of rice for the lord —
offering half, he should set aside the rest for the fire offering. Or in a mandala made before him, adorned with colours,
the teacher should place five pots, in the directions and the centre. In them the one most learned in ritual should establish the Brahmans with the letters of the root mantra, with bindu and nada,
beginning with "nam" and ending with "yam": Ishana in the central pot, Purusha in the one in front,
Aghora in the southern, Vama in the northern and Sadya in the western. Having made protection, bound the gesture and consecrated the pots,
he should begin the fire offering in the Shiva fire as before. The half of the sweet rice set aside earlier for the offering —
having offered it, he should set aside the rest for the disciple to eat. Having performed the rite up to the satisfying of the mantras as before,
Kala, principle, world, letter, word and mantra — in brief, these are recited as the six paths.
and having offered their full oblation, he should then perform the kindling: after Om, "hum," then the root mantra ending in "phat,"
ending in "svaha," they declare for kindling, and the limbs in order; three oblations of them should be given in the rite of kindling.
With those mantras one by one their blazing forms should be contemplated. A white thread spun by a brahmin maiden, tripled and tripled again,
consecrating thread with thread, he should tie to the tip of the novice's tuft, letting it hang down to the big toe while he stands erect,
and there join it with the sushumna. Taking it with the peaceful gesture and the root mantra, the mantra-knower,
having offered three oblations, should establish its presence. Striking the disciple on the heart with a toss of flowers as before,
taking up his consciousness and placing it at the end of twelve, joining thread with thread and protecting it with the weapon and armour mantras,
veiling it, he should contemplate the thread as the disciple's body, and contemplate in it the noose made of the three impurities, marked by enjoyment and the enjoyable,
producing objects, senses, body and the like. The kalas beginning with Shantyatita, in the form of the elements beginning with space,
should be joined in the thread by their own names and worshipped with "namah"; or doing the aforesaid with their seed syllables in order,
The five kalas beginning with Nivritti are called the path of kalas by the wise; the other five paths are pervaded by the five kalas.

he should then observe the pervasion of the impurity and the rest in the principles and the rest, and the pervasion of the kalas in the impurity and the rest; having made offerings, he should kindle the kalas.
Striking the disciple on the head and on the thread on the body in order, he should mark the thread at the station of Shantyatita, uttering the mantra.
Having done so from Shantyatita down to Nivritti in order, and offered three oblations, he should then worship Shiva in the mandala.
Seating the disciple to the right of the god, facing north, in a mandala with darbha, the guru should give him the charu left over from the offering.
The disciple, honouring what the guru gives, preceded by Shiva's name, having eaten it and then sipped water twice, should utter the Shiva mantra.
In another mandala the guru should likewise give him the five products of the cow; he too, drinking as he is able and sipping twice, should remember Shiva.
Seating the disciple in a third mandala as before, he should give him a tooth-stick with the characteristics stated in the shastra.
With its soft end, facing east or north, restraining speech and seated, the disciple should clean his teeth.
Washing the tooth-stick, throwing it away and sipping water, he should remember Shiva; directed by the teacher, he should enter Shiva's mandala with folded hands.
If the discarded tooth-stick is seen by the guru to point east, north or west, it is auspicious; otherwise, inauspicious.
From the Shiva principle down to earth is declared the path of principles, twenty-six in number, both pure and impure.
If it faces an inauspicious direction, to allay that fault the guru should offer a hundred, fifty or twenty-five oblations with the root mantra.
Then, touching the disciple and whispering "Shiva" into his ears, he should have that disciple stay overnight on the right side of the god.
On a bed of darbha spread with new cloth, consecrated with mantras, pure, meditating on Shiva within, he should sleep at night with his head to the east.
Tying the tuft of the one whose tuft bears the thread with his own tuft, the guru should cover him with new cloth and the armour mantra,
and making three lines around with ash, sesame and mustard over which the weapon mantra has been recited, he should offer bali outside to the lords of the directions.
The disciple too, fasting thereafter and having thus kept the overnight rite, on waking and rising should tell the guru the dream he has seen.
From the Adhara to the Unmana is declared the path of worlds, sixty in number without its divisions and subdivisions.
The fifty letters in the form of Rudras are called the path of letters; the path of words is declared to have many divisions.
The path of mantras is pervaded by all the subsidiary mantras and the supreme knowledge. Just as Shiva, the leader of the principles, is not counted among the principles,
so he, the leader of mantras, is not counted in the path of mantras. The pervasiveness of the path of kalas and the pervadedness of the other paths —
whoever does not know this truly is not worthy of purifying the paths. One by whom the form of the six paths is not known
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 18: the account of the purification of the six paths and so on. Upamanyu said: Then, having completed bathing and everything, directed by the teacher, he should go with folded hands, meditating, beside Shiva's mandala.
Then, taking it with the root mantra and the gesture seen in the shastra, the teacher should mentally join it at once to all wombs:
the eight classes of gods, the five classes of animals and the one class of humans — fourteen wombs.
For the novice's simultaneous entry into all of them, he should mentally place the disciple's self in Vagishvari as is right.
For the completion of the embryo, having worshipped and bowed to the god and made offerings as is right, he should remember it as completed.
For the one so completed, he should by the rite bring about birth and continuance, uprightness, the attainment of enjoyment, and supreme delight.
For expiation and for accomplishing the sacraments of birth, life and enjoyment, the excellent teacher should offer three oblations and entreat the god.
Having thus purified the impurity of attachment to enjoyership and its objects, and the body, he should then cut the disciple's three nooses.
By the utter severance of the noose that binds him tight, he should regard the disciple's consciousness as pure and alone.
Having offered the full oblation in the fire, he should then worship Brahma; offering him three oblations, he should convey to him Shiva's command:
Grandsire, you must place no obstacle in the way of this one going to Shiva's supreme state; this is Shiva's weighty command.
Then, having done everything except the worship as on the previous day, up to the binding of the eyes, the guru should show him the mandala.
Having commanded thus and worshipped him, he should dismiss him according to rule; having worshipped Mahadeva, he should offer three oblations.
Raising the disciple's self, purified by Nivritti, as before, and placing it in himself and in the thread, he should then worship Vagisha.
Offering three oblations to him, bowing and dismissing her, he should join Nivritti with Pratishtha, together with its kala.
At the joining, having performed worship at once and offered three oblations, he should then contemplate the entry of the disciple's self into Pratishtha.
Then, invoking Pratishtha and doing all the rest described before, he should contemplate its pervasion and Vagishani pervading it,
like the orb of the full moon; doing the rest as before, he should convey to Vishnu the command of Shiva, the supreme self.
Having done the dismissal of Vishnu and the rest, and with Vidya the remainder, joining Pratishtha and doing in it as before,
contemplating its pervasion and Vagisha in order, having done everything up to the full oblation in the blazing fire, and the rest as before,
establishing Nilarudra, performing worship and the like for him, he should give him Shiva's command by the path described.
Dismissing him too and performing rites for his peace, and establishing the Vidya kala, he should observe its pervasion,
When the blindfolded disciple has scattered flowers, the name of the deity on which the flowers fall he should give him.
and likewise Vagishi pervading his own self as before, resembling the morning sun, illuminating the ten directions.
Then, doing the rest as before, invoking and worshipping the god Maheshvara and making offerings to him, he should mentally convey Shiva's command.
Likewise dismissing Maheshvara and doing this other kala, leading on to the Shantyatita kala, he should observe its pervasion,
and likewise contemplate Vagishi pervading his own self, like the expanse of the sky, and everything up to the full oblation as before.
Having done the rest according to the rule and worshipped Sadashiva, he should convey to him the command of Shambhu of boundless deeds.
There too, as before, having worshipped Shiva on the head as before and Vagisha, he should bow and dismiss them.
Then, sprinkling the disciple on the head with Shiva as before, he should contemplate the dissolution of Shantyatita into the Shakti principle.
He should contemplate the supreme Shaiva Shakti, beyond the six paths, pervading all paths, radiant as ten million suns.
Bringing the disciple before it, spotless as pure crystal, and washing the scissors, then by the path described in the Shiva shastra
the teacher should cut off his tuft together with the thread; then placing it in cow-dung, he should offer the tuft into the Shiva fire.
Bringing him into this mandala of offerings as before, he should worship the god Ishana and make offerings in the Shiva fire.
With the root mantra ending in "vaushat," washing the scissors again, he should return the disciple's consciousness into his body in his hand.
Then, the novice having bathed, sipped water and had blessings pronounced, he should bring him near the mandala, and he should prostrate like a staff.
Having performed worship as is right, for the purification of any defect in the rites he should offer three oblations with the spoken mantra;
he should offer three oblations with whispered utterance; again worshipping the lord of gods, for the purification of any defect in the mantras,

he should offer three oblations with mental utterance. There, having worshipped Shambhu in the mandala together with Amba and offered three oblations, the guru should then entreat him with folded hands:
Lord, by your grace the purification of this one's six paths has been done; therefore lead him to your supreme, imperishable abode.
Having thus informed the god, preceded by the joining of the channels, and done everything up to the full oblation as before, he should then purify the elements.
For purification then, in the stable and unstable, and in the cold and hot states, he should meditate on oneness through pervasion in the rite of purifying the elements.
Having cut the knots of the elements and let them go with their rulers, whoever by the yoga of stability recites the elements in the supreme Shiva,
having purified the face, burned the body and flooded it with drops of nectar, and established the self, should then make the body consist of the purified paths.
If the disciple has seen a bad dream, then to allay that fault he should offer a hundred, fifty or twenty-five oblations with the root knowledge.
There, first, he should place on the novice's head the Shantyatita kala, pervading his own path, pure, and likewise the Shanti on the face;
the Vidya from the throat to the navel, the Pratishtha below that in order, down to the knees, and below that he should place Nivritti and contemplate it.
Placing the thread-mantra with its seeds and limbs, understanding him to be of the nature of Shiva, he should invoke the god in the lotus of his heart and worship him.
Praying for Shiva's constant presence and Shiva's selfhood in the novice, the guru should bestow qualities on this novice, who is made of Shiva's radiance:
saying "Be gracious," he should give three oblations for the powers beginning with anima; and in the same way bestow on him again the qualities:
omniscience, contentment, knowledge without beginning or end, undiminished power, freedom and infinite power.
Then, taking leave of the god, he should sprinkle him with the pots beginning with Sadya, meditating on the lord of gods in his heart in order.
Then, seating that disciple and worshipping Shiva as before, having received permission from Shiva, he should teach him the Shaiva knowledge,
preceded by Omkara, enclosed and ending with "namah," joined with Shiva and Shakti, and the Shakti knowledge of the same kind.
He should teach the seer, metre and deity, the Shiva-ness of the two, the worship of Shambhu with its enclosures, and the seats.
Then, letting the thread tied to the tuft hang down as before, beginning with the worship of the support, everything relating to the Nivritti kala,
Worshipping the lord of gods again, he should inform Shiva: "Make all that I have performed well done."
The guru, with the disciple, bowing to the god like a staff on the ground, should dismiss him from the mandala and from the fire.
Then all the members of the assembly who are worthy of honour should be honoured in order;
the members of the assembly and the officiating priests should be served according to one's wealth; one should not be niggardly with wealth if one desires Shiva for oneself.
up to the worship of Vageshvari, he should perform, preceded by the fire offering. Then, bowing to Vagisha and to the chaste one who pervades Nivritti,
worshipping the god in the mandala and offering three oblations, he should bring about the novice's attainment in all wombs at once.
Then, on the thread-body of the disciple, having performed striking, sprinkling and the like, and taking up his self and placing it at the end of twelve,
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 19: the greatness of the mantra of the sacrament of the practitioner. Upamanyu said: Next I shall tell of the sacrament called Sadhaka by name, and the greatness of the mantra, which I indicated in the telling.
The practice of the mantra need not be pursued to the utmost by one seeking liberation; but if done, it brings good to him too, here and elsewhere.
On an auspicious day, in an auspicious place, or at a time free of faults, with clean teeth and nails, bathed, having performed the morning rites,
adorned with whatever fragrance, garlands and ornaments are available, with turban and upper garment, all in white, collected,
in a temple, a house or some other very lovely place, seated comfortably in a posture practised before,
having made his body Shaiva by the path described in the Shiva shastra and worshipped the Lord Nakulishvara, lord of the god of gods,
offering him sweet rice and completing the worship in order, bowing to that god and receiving permission from his mouth,
he should recite Shiva's mantra ten million times, or half that, or half again, or two million, or one million times.
Then, eating a measured meal of sweet rice without pungent things or salt, he should always be non-violent, forbearing, peaceful and self-controlled.
If sweet rice is not available, he may eat fruits, roots and the like enjoined by Shiva, each better than the one before:
charu, food, barley meal and grains, barley gruel, vegetables, milk, curd, ghee, roots, fruits and water.
Having worshipped the god in the mandala and placed him in the pot as before, and made offerings, he should bring the disciple without turban onto the ground in the mandala.
Consecrating the foods and the like with the mantra, in this practice especially he should always eat in silence.
The observer of the vow should bathe in clean water purified by the mantra recited a hundred and eight times, from a river or stream, or sprinkle himself according to his ability.
He should likewise make libations daily and offer into the Shiva fire with seven, five or three substances, or with ghee alone.
For the Shaiva practitioner who thus attains Shiva by devotion, nothing is hard to obtain here or hereafter.
Or else, one-pointed in mind, he should recite the mantra a thousand times every day while fasting, even without the practice of the mantra.
For him nothing is hard to obtain and there is never anything inauspicious; having gained learning, fortune and happiness here, he attains liberation.
In the practice, in its application, in the daily and occasional rites, he should recite after bathing with water and with ash and with the mantra in order.
Pure, with tuft tied, wearing the thread, with the purifying ring on his hand, wearing tripundra and rudraksha, he should recite the five-syllabled knowledge.
Having done everything up to the full oblation as before and offered a hundred oblations, the excellent teacher, having satisfied with the root mantra and the pots,
and kindled as before, and done in order what was described before, sprinkling him as before, should give him the excellent mantra.
There, having done everything in order at length up to the teaching of knowledge, he should place the Shaiva knowledge in the novice's hand with flower-water:
This great mantra will surely grant you the fruit of every success in this world and the next, by the grace of the Supreme.
Having said this and worshipped the god, the guru, receiving leave from Shiva, should teach the practitioner the practice and Shiva-yoga.
Hearing the guru's instruction, the mantra practitioner should in order perform the practice of the mantra before its application.
The practice of the root mantra is called the preparatory rite, since it must be performed before the rite called application.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 20: the special sacraments and others. Upamanyu said: Then, the disciple having been thus sanctified and having kept the Pashupata vow, one should consecrate him to the office of teacher if he is fit, and otherwise not.
Then, having adorned him and worshipped the god in the Shiva mandala, offering a hundred and eight oblations, he should give the full oblation.
Again worshipping the lord of gods and bowing on the ground like a staff, placing his folded hands on his head, the guru should inform Shiva:
Lord, by your grace I have made this one a teacher; favour him, O God, and grant him your divine command.
Having so informed him and bowed again with the disciple, the guru should worship Shiva and the divine Shiva Agama as Shiva himself.
Again taking Shiva's leave, the teacher should give the book of Shiva's knowledge to the disciple with both hands.
He, placing that knowledge on his head and setting it on the seat of knowledge, should salute and worship it as is right.
Then the guru should give him the insignia of royalty too, since one who has attained the teacher's rank deserves a kingdom as well.
Then he should instruct him as the ancients practised, as stated in the Shiva shastra, and as is honoured in the world:
Having carefully examined disciples by the marks described in the Shiva shastra and sanctified them, the teacher should give them the knowledge of Shiva.
Thus he should diligently cultivate effortlessness in all things, purity, forbearance, compassion, freedom from craving and from envy.
Having made the mandala as before and worshipped the supreme Lord, he should place five pots, in the directions and in the centre as before.
Having thus instructed that disciple and dismissed Shiva from the mandala, he should worship the Shiva pot, the fire and the rest, and the members of the assembly.
Or the guru with his assistants may perform the sacraments together; there, three or two are taught for use.
Then at the very beginning he should prepare the pots as for the purification of the paths; having performed the samaya sacrament, all except the sprinkling,
and having worshipped Shiva again and performed the purification of the paths — when that is completed he should worship the god again,
offer the mantra, satisfy it, kindle it and pray to the Lord; placing the mantra in the disciple's hand, he should finish the rest.
Or, contemplating the whole mantra sacrament in order, the guru should perform the purification of the paths ending in the sprinkling.
The rite enjoined there for the kalas beginning with Shantyatita should all be performed in the purification of the three principles.
The three principles are declared to be Shiva, Vidya and Atma. From Shiva in Shakti arose Vidya, and from her the Atma.
By Shiva the path of Shantyatita is pervaded, and the other, the higher; by Vidya the remaining path; by the Atma the whole in order.
The wise, masters of the meaning of the Shiva shastras, regarding the Shambhava initiation, the root of the mantra, as hard to attain, should commend the Shakti sacrament.
Placing Nivritti in front, Pratishtha in the western pot, Vidya in the south, Shanti in the north and the Supreme in the middle,
Thus I have told you all of the rite called sacrament, O Krishna, in its four kinds; what more do you wish to hear?
having made protection and the rest there, bound the cow gesture, consecrated the pots and offered everything up to the full oblation as before,
the teacher should lead the disciple without turban into the mandala and perform the satisfying of the mantras and the rest, ending as before.
Then, having worshipped the lord of gods and taken leave as before, he should seat the disciple on the seat for sprinkling.
Then, having made him whole as the embodiment of the five kalas, his body placed with mantras, having bound him, he should offer the disciple to Shiva.
Then, lifting in order the pots beginning with the Nivritti pot, ending with the middle one, he should sprinkle the disciple with Shiva's mantra.
Then, placing Shiva's hand on the novice's head, the teacher, filled with the state of Shiva, should appoint him a Shaiva teacher.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

With a cow's horn with darbha, or a palasha or lotus leaf, or with both hands, five times or three,
in a garden and the like, or at home, with a vardhani vessel or a pot; at the time of immersion he should sprinkle himself with water consecrated by mantras.
If he is unable to perform the water bath, he should cleanse his body from the soles of the feet to the head with a clean wet cloth.
Or he may take the fire bath or the mantra bath, or bathe with Shiva; a bath devoted to thinking of Shiva is called the yogi's own bath.
By the rule stated in his own sutra, preceded by sipping with mantras, having made libations to the gods and others, he should perform everything up to the Brahma sacrifice.
Meditating on Mahadeva in the orb and worshipping him according to rule, he should then offer arghya to Shiva in the form of the sun.
Or, having done this as stated in his own sutra, he should purify his hands; then performing the placing on the hands, his body made whole,
with water held in his left hand mixed with fragrance and white mustard, or sprinkling with a bunch of kusha, with the root mantra,
with the mantras beginning "apo hi shtha," and smelling the remaining water through the left nostril, he should contemplate the god as white.
Upamanyu said: Rising from bed at dawn and meditating on the god with Amba, having considered his tasks, he should go out of the house when the dawn has risen.
Taking the arghya, he should contemplate what is in the body, through the right nostril, as dark in colour, as outside and placed on a stone.
Then he should make libations to the gods and especially to the sages, and give arghya to beings and ancestors according to rule.
With water of red sandal he should make on the ground a well-rounded mandala the size of a hand, adorned with red powder and the like.
There he should worship the sun together with its own enclosures, with the mantra "khakholkaya" and its limbs, for the attainment of happiness.
Again making a mandala and worshipping its limbs, he should place there a golden vessel measuring a Magadha prastha,
and fill it with fragrant water mixed with red sandal, red flowers and sesame, with kusha and unbroken grains,
with durva, apamarga and cow products, or with plain water; kneeling on the ground and bowing to the god in the orb,
placing the vessel on his head, he should give that arghya to Shiva; or with cupped hands he should toss up water with darbha, with the root knowledge,
to Shiva in the sky, in the form of the sun. Again performing the placing on the hands, preceded by the purification of the hands,
understanding Shiva as made of the five Brahmans from Ishana to Sadya, taking ash with the mantras, he should rub and touch his limbs:
In an unobstructed, lonely place he should then do the necessary; having cleansed himself according to rule, he should clean his teeth.

putting it on and sipping twice, sprinkling with water consecrated with the eleven mantras, covering himself with another cloth and sipping twice, he should remember Shiva.
Again placing mantras on his hands, the mantra-knower should draw the tripundra with ash, clearly and without crookedness on the forehead with scented water.
Whatever mark he draws with ash on the forehead — round, square, a dot or a half-moon —
the same he should draw on the arms, the head and between the breasts. Smearing the whole body with ash is not equal to the tripundra;
therefore he should draw the tripundra alone, without the smearing. He should wear rudraksha on the head, throat, ears and hands,
golden in colour, unbroken, auspicious, not worn by others; for brahmins and the others in order the best are yellow, red and black.
If those are not available, he should wear whatever is available, undamaged; even then, what is proper to the higher should not be worn by the lower, nor the lower by the higher.
He should not wear the beads when impure, but wear them at all times. Thus, three times a day, or twice, or even once,
having bathed and the rest according to his ability, he should worship the supreme Lord. Going to the place of worship and taking a pleasant seat,

Again bowing to the god Shiva, he should then recite the eight names: Shiva, Maheshvara, Rudra, Vishnu, Pitamaha,
Samsaravaidya, Sarvajna and Paramatman — these eight; or else recite "Shiva" alone eleven times or more.

Meditating on a mass of radiance on the tip of the tongue for the quelling of disease and the like, washing his feet and anointing his hands with sandal, he should perform the placing on the hands, preceded by their purification.
Having sipped water according to rule, he should then take the water bath, in a river, a temple tank, a lake or at home.
Placing the bathing things on the bank and removing outer dirt, smearing himself with clay and bathing, he should smear himself with cow-dung.
Bathing again and again, discarding or washing his garment, well bathed like a king, he should put on a clean garment again.
A student, an ascetic and a widow should not take the cleansing bath, the bath with perfumes and the like, or clean the teeth.
Wearing the sacred thread and tying his tuft, entering the water and immersing himself, having sipped water, he should draw three circles in the water.
Salutations to Shri Ganesha.
Salutations to Shri Gauri and Shankara.

The glorious Shiva Mahapurana, book 7, part 2, chapter 22: the description of the daily and occasional rites taught in the Shiva shastras. Upamanyu said: The placing of mantras is declared threefold, in the order of maintenance, creation and dissolution: maintenance is for householders, creation for students,
He should join the self, impelled by the vital breath through the sushumna channel and gone out through the aperture of Brahman, with Shiva's radiance.
Having dried the body with air, he should then burn it with the fire of time; then, in the upward course, withdrawing the kalas with air,
withdrawing the burned body, touching the kalas with their ruler, flooding the body with nectar, he should restore it to its place.
Or, having withdrawn and burned it without re-creating the kalas, he should then flood what has become ash with nectar.
Then, in that body made of knowledge, he should join the self, shaped like a lamp-flame, come forth from Shiva, through the aperture of Brahman.
Meditating on it as having entered the body, in the lotus of the heart, he should again sprinkle the body made of knowledge with a rain of nectar.
Then he should perform the placing on the hands, preceded by their purification, and afterwards the placing on the body with the great gesture.
Then, having performed the placing on the limbs by the path taught by Shiva, he should perform the placing of letters on the joints of hands, feet and the rest.
Then, placing the six limbs with the six classes, he should afterwards perform the binding of the directions, beginning with the south-east in order.
